section_summary: This section closes a Spanish-language Japanese propaganda compilation with articles on Soviet-Japanese rivalry and Japan’s imperial, Shinto, and cultural identity. The remaining documents, chiefly from 1937–1938, concern alleged Japanese espionage, surveying, economic penetration, fishing operations, alien smuggling, petroleum ambitions, and possible naval facilities in Mexico, especially Baja California and northern Mexico. They also document State, War, and Post Office Department inquiries into Japanese-American newspapers and individuals in San Francisco, alongside several unverified public allegations and duplicated intelligence reports.

subfiles.title: El Soviet y el Japón (conclusion)
subfiles.from: Unnamed author; reprinted by El Universal
subfiles.about: Analyzes the military and diplomatic balance between Japan and the Soviet Union and recommends a guarded Japanese policy.
subfiles.summary: Conclusion of El Soviet y el Japon: Soviet industrialization, rearmament and alliances, tensions over Manchukuo-Mongolia and North China; immediate war is not inevitable, and Japan should settle disputes.

subfiles.title: El Alma del Japón
subfiles.from: Unnamed author; reprinted by El Universal
subfiles.about: Presents imperial loyalty and Shinto-derived national identity as the enduring essence of Japan.
subfiles.summary: The article argues that Buddhism, Confucianism, and Western civilization altered Japan’s outward culture without changing its essential reverence for the emperor and imperial house. It credits native-learning scholars such as Hirata Atsutane with reviving Shinto doctrines that helped undermine the shogunate. Western individualism is portrayed as incompatible with Japan’s national spirit.

subfiles.title: Índice of Spanish-language Japanese compilation
subfiles.about: Lists the compilation’s articles on Japanese society, politics, culture, trade, militarism, and international relations.
subfiles.summary: Index of a Spanish-language Japanese compilation, from medicine and women's roles to military spirit and Soviet-Japanese relations.

subfiles.title: Report regarding the Activities of Japanese in Lower California
subfiles.doc_type: consular report; enclosure to Despatch No. 69
subfiles.from: William A. Smale, American Consul at Ensenada
subfiles.about: Reports alleged Japanese intelligence gathering, economic penetration, fishing expansion, and alien smuggling in Baja California.
subfiles.summary: Smale argues that Japanese residents and visitors in Baja California were collecting maps, charts, terrain measurements, and other information potentially useful in war. He describes Japanese organization in Ensenada, Tijuana, and the Maneadero Valley, estimates the Japanese population and recent illegal arrivals, and contends that fishing vessels facilitated unlawful entry into the United States. The report also alleges expanding Mitsui influence over Mexico’s abalone and marine-products industries.

subfiles.title: Letter on Japanese fishermen and the O/S SENATOR
subfiles.to: District Director of Immigration, Los Angeles
subfiles.about: Warns that the fishing vessel SENATOR may recruit Japanese crews at unmonitored Baja California ports.
subfiles.summary: Smale explains doubts that Japanese fishermen Captain Dickason sought to hire were bona fide seamen, warning recruitment at Cedros Island or Turtle Bay could undermine immigration control and allow intelligence gathering.

subfiles.title: H. M. Newhall & Co. inquiry about a Japanese-Mexican fishery
subfiles.from: H. J. Steele, H. M. Newhall & Co.
subfiles.to: Marine Products Company, attention L. K. Small
subfiles.about: Requests an assessment of reports that Japanese and Mexican interests planned a joint fishery.
subfiles.summary: H. M. Newhall asks whether a reported Mexican venture with Japanese trawlers in the Gulf of California could affect the canned-abalone business.

subfiles.title: Marine Products Company letter on Mitsui and Japanese fishing plans
subfiles.from: L. K. Small, Marine Products Company
subfiles.to: Cia. de Productos Marinos, S.A., attention Miguel Candara
subfiles.about: Reports discussions with Shin Shibata about Mitsui’s pricing advantage and Japanese involvement in Mexican fisheries.
subfiles.summary: Marine Products Company reports Shibata acknowledging Mitsui's advantage in the Oriental market, two trawlers being built in Japan for Mexico, and Mexican youths trained in Japan.

subfiles.title: Marine Products Company letter to William C. Morehead
subfiles.from: L. K. Small, Marine Products Company
subfiles.to: William C. Morehead, Pacific Ocean Products, Ltd.
subfiles.about: Challenges a reported low-price abalone contract between Coronado Fisheries and Mitsui.
subfiles.summary: Small asks Morehead to confirm a report of a Mitsui contract for much of Coronado Fisheries' 1937 Turtle Bay abalone pack at a price advantage.

subfiles.title: Coronado Fisheries reply on the Mitsui abalone agreement
subfiles.from: William C. Morehead, Coronado Fisheries, Inc.
subfiles.to: L. K. Small, Marine Products Company
subfiles.about: Explains the pricing terms of Coronado Fisheries’ abalone arrangement with Mitsui.
subfiles.summary: Morehead says the Mitsui abalone agreement was at $7.50 a case less commission and expenses, and advises sales agents to hold prices and avoid a price war.

subfiles.title: Senator Lodge inquiry concerning an alleged Japanese port at Ensenada
subfiles.about: Asks whether the State Department is monitoring alleged Japanese negotiations for a port concession at Ensenada.
subfiles.summary: Senator Lodge forwards Joseph Perry's letter and clipping and asks for information on a reported Japanese concession at Ensenada.

subfiles.title: Joseph M. Perry letter about Ensenada
subfiles.about: Asks whether the State Department is watching Japanese efforts to obtain an Ensenada concession.
subfiles.summary: Perry asks if Washington is following reported Ensenada negotiations, suggesting even a Honolulu steamship terminal could compete with an American line.

subfiles.title: Suspicions Aroused
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper letter to the editor; clipping
subfiles.about: Warns that German, Italian, and Japanese residents and facilities might become wartime threats inside the United States.
subfiles.summary: Letter to the editor condemning foreign-sponsored military camps and alleging Japan sought bases at Magdalena Bay and Ensenada and a coordinated German-Japanese attack.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on anonymous threats from San Luis Potosí
subfiles.about: Summarizes anonymous letters alleging that Japan intended to attack the Philippines in 1933.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs finds of no special interest a San Luis Potosi despatch reporting insulting anonymous letters and a pseudonymous claim about a Japanese officer.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Lodge
subfiles.about: Responds to the inquiry about a purported Japanese port concession at Ensenada.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Lodge that no report from American representatives in Mexico confirmed the Ensenada allegation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Welles memorandum on Japanese activities
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a memorandum on a conversation with the Mexican ambassador about Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Welles's memorandum: the Mexican ambassador says President Cardenas ordered much stricter supervision of Japanese activities.

subfiles.title: Internal note on Japanese population statistics for Mexico
subfiles.from: Unnamed Division of the American Republics official
subfiles.about: Suggests giving Senator Hayden a telephone estimate of the Japanese population in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Note proposing to advise Senator Hayden by telephone: July information indicated about 5,300 Japanese in Mexico.

subfiles.title: Senator Hayden inquiry on the number of Japanese in Mexico
subfiles.about: Requests diplomatic information on the number of Japanese residents in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Senator Hayden relays a Graham County Chamber of Commerce question on Mexico's Japanese population; the best July 1937 estimate was about 5,300.

subfiles.title: Fort Huachuca intelligence report on Japanese photography near Altar
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese man photographing an emergency landing field and traveling near the border in Sonora.
subfiles.summary: Fort Huachuca report: a rancher saw an unidentified Japanese man photograph the old Pan American emergency field near Altar and appear near Sasabe; passport apparently showed entry at Manzanillo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum summarizing Despatch No. 200 from Chihuahua
subfiles.about: Summarizes Louis Collins’s allegations about Japanese and German surveying parties in northern Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Summary of Despatch No. 200: Collins saw Japanese groups with surveying and communications equipment along the Sonora-Chihuahua border, apparently mapping roads and water, while four Germans questioned him.

subfiles.title: Japanese Army Exploring Parties in Northern Mexico
subfiles.from: Lee R. Blohm, American Consul at Chihuahua
subfiles.about: Transmits Louis Collins’s report of Japanese and German parties apparently surveying northern Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Collins claims several well-equipped Japanese groups moved west from Chihuahua in late 1937, apparently mapping roads, water and airfields; Blohm records similar suspicions of four Germans.

subfiles.title: Japanese Army Exploring Parties in Northern Mexico, duplicate copy
subfiles.from: Lee R. Blohm, American Consul at Chihuahua
subfiles.about: Duplicates the Chihuahua consular despatch transmitting Louis Collins’s allegations.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Collins’s account of several Japanese groups traveling through western Chihuahua with surveying, camping, and electrical equipment. It also repeats his claim that German parties sought information on roads and towns in Chihuahua and Sonora. Distribution annotations show copies for the military attaché and the consulate general.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on an alleged Japanese naval base at Mazatlán
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on alleged Japanese negotiations involving Mazatlán harbor and Pacific-coast iron deposits.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a report that Japan sought an iron concession in exchange for modernizing Mazatlan harbor, with translated newspaper articles.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Dr. V. Tsuru’s petroleum activities
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch concerning Dr. V. Tsuru’s petroleum activities around Tampico.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Daniels transmits the Tampico consul's report on the Japanese Dr. V. Tsuru's activities in the petroleum region.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities in Baja California
subfiles.about: Reports unfamiliar Japanese men photographing and observing Ensenada and Todos Santos Bay.
subfiles.summary: Smale reports nonresident Japanese visitors photographing and using field glasses around Ensenada; two men he met falsely claimed local residence. He advises not dismissing espionage.

subfiles.title: White House referral of H. Russell Brand correspondence
subfiles.from: Marvin H. McIntyre, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: Refers H. Russell Brand’s correspondence for acknowledgment and consideration.
subfiles.summary: White House referral cover sheet on H. Russell Brand's letterhead forwarding his warnings about Japanese influence in Mexico.

subfiles.title: H. Russell Brand letter to Senator Hiram Johnson
subfiles.about: Urges an immediate campaign against alleged Japanese influence in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Brand praises Senator Johnson's anti-Japanese record, calls Japanese activity in Mexico urgent, and alleges Japan evades Monroe Doctrine restraints.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to H. Russell Brand
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Brand’s White House-referred letter about Japanese influence in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Brand's letter to the president enclosing his note to Senator Johnson, which received careful consideration.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on investigating the New World editor
subfiles.about: Records a decision to investigate allegations about the editor of a Japanese newspaper.
subfiles.summary: Tanis and Sturgeon agreed Bannerman should examine the New World editor's activities; meanwhile Hubert Malone should receive an acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s referral of Malone’s letter
subfiles.about: Suggests referring Malone’s allegations to R. C. Bannerman and the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Welles forwards an incoming letter, recommending coordination with the chief special agent and Far Eastern Affairs.

subfiles.title: Post Office letter transmitting New World investigation
subfiles.from: C. W. Pfeffenberger, Post Office Inspector in Charge
subfiles.to: R. C. Bannerman, Chief Special Agent
subfiles.about: Transmits an investigation into the Japanese newspaper New World and its personnel.
subfiles.summary: Pfeffenberger says Inspector Austin investigated in San Francisco on April 7 and 8 and encloses his memorandum and exhibits.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the New World-Sun and Kakuzo Ichimaru
subfiles.from: G. H. Austin, Post Office Inspector
subfiles.to: C. W. Pfeffenberger and R. C. Bannerman
subfiles.about: Investigates the ownership, management, circulation, and immigration histories associated with the New World-Sun.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum traces the New World newspaper from 1894 to its 1935 merger into the New World-Sun and examines Ichimaru's and Hara's records; Austin found no evidence of Ichimaru's alleged Japanese naval connection.

subfiles.title: New World-Sun newspaper exhibit
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper exhibit; largely illegible in OCR
subfiles.about: Represents the newspaper issue enclosed as an exhibit with the Post Office investigation.
subfiles.summary: Exhibit page, an April 6, 1938 issue of the New World-Sun, almost wholly unreadable.

subfiles.title: Statement of Ownership, Management, and Circulation of The New World-Sun
subfiles.to: Postmaster and Third Assistant Postmaster General
subfiles.about: Declares the New World-Sun’s management, stockholders, security interests, and circulation.
subfiles.summary: Ownership statement for The New World-Sun naming senior staff and stockholders, with no major bondholders and average paid circulation of 9,501; notarized November 1937.

subfiles.title: Notice of consolidation creating The New World-Sun
subfiles.about: Notifies the postmaster that two Japanese newspapers would merge as The New World-Sun.
subfiles.summary: Hara announces The New World Daily News and The Hokubei Asahi will consolidate, with the first issue under the new title on June 20, 1935.

subfiles.title: Supplemental Post Office letter on the New World
subfiles.from: C. W. Pfeffenberger, Post Office Inspector in Charge
subfiles.to: R. C. Bannerman, Chief Special Agent
subfiles.about: Forwards additional information concerning the New World newspaper.
subfiles.summary: Pfeffenberger supplements his April 9 letter with a new Inspector Austin memorandum on the newspaper and the Ichimaru family.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Asae Ichimaru’s departure for Japan
subfiles.from: G. H. Austin, Post Office Inspector
subfiles.about: Reports Asae Ichimaru’s planned departure for Japan under a reentry permit.
subfiles.summary: Austin reports Asae Ichimaru would sail for Japan on the Tatsuta Maru on April 16, 1938, with her permit numbers.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Hubert Malone’s letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Malone’s observations about Mexican petroleum and related Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges Hubert Malone's March 26 letter, which was read with interest.

subfiles.title: Hubert Malone letter alleging Japanese petroleum plans, handwritten original
subfiles.about: Relays waterfront rumors linking Japan to Mexican oil development and the editor of the New World newspaper.
subfiles.summary: Malone alleges that Japanese naval and civilian experts visited Acapulco in 1935 and offered to finance pipelines and harbor improvements for transporting Mexican oil. He claims Japanese groups had worked for years toward broader control of Mexican resources and that the New World editor informally represented the Japanese Navy. Acknowledging that his information might be rumor, he urges close surveillance of the editor.

subfiles.title: Hubert Malone letter alleging Japanese petroleum plans, typed copy
subfiles.about: Provides a typed copy of Malone’s allegations about Japanese petroleum, port, and newspaper activities.
subfiles.summary: Typed copy of Malone's letter alleging Japanese warships and specialists visited Mexico's Pacific coast offering to finance pipelines and harbors, with rumors of a German Alaska survey; he urges investigating the New World editor.

subfiles.title: Hubert Malone letter alleging Japanese petroleum plans, duplicate typed copy
subfiles.doc_type: duplicate typed copy of private letter
subfiles.about: Duplicates Malone’s account of alleged Japanese plans involving Mexican oil and Pacific ports.
subfiles.summary: This second copy repeats claims that Japan offered financial and technical support for pipelines and harbor improvements following a 1935 naval visit. It also repeats the assertions about Japanese operatives in Mexico, a German cruiser surveying Alaska, and the New World editor’s supposed naval role.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division routing sheet
subfiles.to: Listed War, Navy, State, and Commerce Department offices
subfiles.about: Routes attached intelligence concerning Japanese activity in Mexico for information and filing.
subfiles.summary: Military Intelligence Division routing sheet listing recipients, stamped April, for information and record.

subfiles.title: First Cavalry Division letter on Japanese movements west of Chihuahua
subfiles.from: Unnamed major, General Staff, Headquarters First Cavalry Division
subfiles.to: Major Malcolm Y. Lindsey, Assistant Chief of Staff, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: Reports J. Louis Collins’s allegations that organized Japanese groups were surveying routes across northern Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Collins reports Japanese groups leaving Chihuahua City for the Sierra Madre and coast in late 1937 with compasses and funds, likely government agents interested in roads and trails; motive unclear.
